DOM207 · Batch 8a · Lect-TTest-1 + Lect-TTest-2

The t-test

Small samples, unknown σ, and two questions: did it change, and do the groups differ?

Jaideep Ghosh, The t-test (Lect-TTest-1, 40 slides) and The t-test: "t-test in R" (Lect-TTest-2, 24 slides). School of Management and Entrepreneurship, Shiv Nadar University. DOM207 Introduction to Data Science for Business Using R and Python, Monsoon 2026.

TTest-1 in one breath. The t-test is a top-down, hypothesis-testing procedure for two kinds of business problem. A pre-post problem measures the same people before and after an intervention, and needs the paired t-test. An independent-sample problem compares two unrelated groups, such as control and experimental, and needs the two-sample t-test. Gosset ("Student") built the t distribution in 1908 at Guinness for small samples with an unknown population SD. It is bell-shaped with heavier tails and is governed by degrees of freedom; past n ≈ 30 it is effectively normal. The deck works a one-sample example (t = 2, keep H₀), two HCL training cases in Excel (paired: reject; two-sample: fail to reject), and a pooled-variance pedagogy example (t ≈ 4.28, reject). Unequal variances call for a different test.

TTest-2 in one breath. The same test in R. Male and female score vectors (means 24.5 vs 26.7) go through t.test(), first with equal variances (t = −2.3016, df = 38, p = 0.027) and then as a Welch test (df = 37.801, p = 0.027). Both reject equal means. Normality is checked with Shapiro-Wilk (p = 0.65, 0.74) and histograms. Variance equality is checked with Levene, Fligner-Killeen and the F-based var.test (F = 0.865, p = 0.75).

Deck 1 of 2 · Lect-TTest-1 · 40 slides

The t-test: problems, theory and Excel

Builds on B07 (hypothesis testing: H₀, H₁, α, p-value, Type I error), B06 (mean, variance, SD, boxplots) and the normal distribution and CLT from Inferential Statistics. No data file from Data Files/ is used, except mtcars in the boxplot line (R's built-in copy). The Excel worksheets shown in sl. 27 and 38 are not in the folder.

1–2slides

Opening question

1The t-test2For what types of real-life problems should you use the top-down DSA procedure called the t-test?

The deck opens on a question rather than a definition: which real-life problems does the t-test solve? The answer is two problem types (sl. 3–13). "Top-down DSA" means the approach that starts from a hypothesis and tests it against data, as distinct from bottom-up pattern-finding (sl. 14).

3–7slides

The 1st type of problem: pre-post

3The 1st Type of Problem4Example Application – 15Example Application – 26Example Application – 37Pre-Post Application
Ghosh · sl. 3

A type of problem "encountered in many DS and analytics applications in many fields and disciplines": "A system is originally in some state. Then something external happens to it. The state of the system is modified", and it is either improved or worsened. "Can you check with confidence if one or the other is a significant effect?"

Training sl. 4

An organization is concerned about its workers' job performance. Initially it measures performance with some numerical measure, then gives the employees a training program, then measures the same employees again. Question: has performance improved, i.e. has the training made a difference?

Memory drug sl. 5

A pharmaceutical company records patients' memory scores on a standardised scale, administers the drug, and after a few weeks measures again on the same scale. Has memory improved?

Teaching method sl. 6

SNU performs an education study in which students' scores on a standardized test are recorded. It adopts a new teaching method; afterwards, scores on the same test are recorded (different questions, of course). NOTE: assume the test's difficulty is the same both times. Has the method made a difference?

Pre-post application

sl. 7
Names
Pre-post t-test = paired sample t-test = dependent t-test (sl. 18 adds matched-sample and repeated-measure t-test).
Purpose
Determine if there is a significant difference between the average values of two related measurements.
Typical use
Before-and-after studies: the same group is measured twice, once before the intervention (the pre-test) and once after (the post-test).
8–13slides

The 2nd type of problem: independent samples

8The 2nd Type of Problem9Control Group and Experimental Group10Example Application – 111Example Application – 212Example Application – 313Independent Sample Application

There are two populations (for example, two groups). Samples are taken from each and tested on the numerical value of one characteristic both groups possess [sic: "both group possess"]. You check whether that value is the same or different between the groups (sl. 8).

Control vs experimental sl. 9

In experimental research the experimental group receives the intervention; the control group does not. Comparing the two isolates the intervention's impact and establishes a cause-and-effect relationship.

Cancer drug trial sl. 10

Experimental group gets a new cancer drug; control gets a placebo, "an inactive substance, like a sugar pill, that's given to a patient or subject as if it were a real treatment". Question: is the experimental group's average survival rate significantly higher?

Tyre screws sl. 11

A manufacturing company wants to ensure two different production lines produce car tire screws of the same weight, so it weighs samples of screws from each line. Question: is the average weight from the two lines significantly different?

Teaching Method A vs B sl. 12

SNU wants to compare the effectiveness of Method A and Method B for 2nd-year BMS students. It trains independent samples by each method; their exam scores are collected. Question: is there a significant difference in average scores between the methods?

Independent sample application

sl. 13
Test
Independent sample t-test: compares the means of two separate, unrelated groups to see if they are significantly different.
When
When you want to answer "whether a difference observed in sample data reflects a true difference in the main population".
Also called
Two-sample t-test, independent t-test (sl. 18).

outside slidesQuick sort: if each number in group 1 has a partner in group 2 from the same person or item, it is paired (sl. 3–7). If the groups are different people or items, it is independent (sl. 8–13). The SNU teaching example appears in both: sl. 6 is the same students before and after (paired); sl. 12 is two separate groups (independent).

14–18slides

t-tests and hypothesis testing in a nutshell

14t-tests15HT in a Nutshell – 116HT in a Nutshell – 217HT in a Nutshell – 318t-tests Details

These are "very popular applications in DSA", and the technique for them is the t-test, "an example of the top-down approach to DSA based on hypothesis testing (HT)" (sl. 14).

Nutshell 1 sl. 15

In HT you test an assumption about a population using sample data. First the null hypothesis (H₀): "a default assumption of no effect or something everybody knows and is uninteresting". Then the alternative hypothesis (H₁): "a claim of an interesting or surprising effect or difference".

Nutshell 2 sl. 16

Analyse the sample to see if there is enough evidence to reject the null and support the alternative, i.e. whether the pattern is a real population effect or just random chance. If you reject the null, you have discovered an "interesting/surpsiing [→ surprising] effect".

Nutshell 3 sl. 17

To perform the test you need two things. Significance level (SL, α): the probability of incorrectly rejecting a true null (e.g. 0.05 or 5%). p-value: the probability of observing something as extreme as the [sic: "the the"] sample data if the null were true.

Two important actions, among others

sl. 18
Paired means
"Determine if two dependent sample means are different." Called the paired sample t-test, matched sample t-test or repeated measure t-test.
Two groups
"Determine if there is a difference between two groups within the population." Called the two sample t-test or independent t-test.
Decision rule
From B07: reject H₀ when p ≤ α, equivalently when |tcalc| exceeds the critical t (both are used in sl. 24, 27, 37, 38).
19–23slides

History and the t distribution

19t-tests History – 120t-tests History – 221What's the t Distribution?22Characteristics of t Distribution23t Distribution (figure)
Ghosh · sl. 19

"In 1908 William Sealy Gosset, an Englishman publishing under the pseudonym Student, developed the t-test and t distribution." Gosset worked at the Guinness brewery in Dublin and found that existing large-sample techniques "were not useful for the small sample sizes that he encountered in his work".

As the sample size increases the t distribution tends to the bell-shaped standard normal. In practice, for tests on the mean of a sample larger than 30, the normal distribution is usually applied (sl. 20). The t distribution, also called Student's t distribution, is a bell-shaped probability curve, appropriate when your sample is small and you do not know the true population SD (sl. 21).

Characteristic (sl. 22)What the slide says
Bell-shaped and symmetricLike the normal, it centres at 0 and is symmetrical.
Heavier tailsShorter and flatter in the middle, with thicker tails than a standard normal (z-score). Extreme values are therefore more likely.
Degrees of freedom (DOF)Its exact shape depends on the sample size through the DOF, n − 1, where n is the sample size.
Large-sample normalityAs sample size and DOF increase, it becomes taller, thinner and nearly identical to the standard normal (usually by n > 30).

Figure, sl. 23: three curves on one axis running from −∞ to ∞ with μ = 0 marked. The tallest, narrowest is the Z distribution (standard normal); a red middle curve is the t-distribution (n close to 30); the flattest, widest is the t-distribution (n smaller than 30). The lab below redraws this with a DOF slider.

outside slidesA slip on sl. 23 itself: the curve labelled "n close to 30" is drawn far shorter than the Z curve, but sl. 22 says that by n ≈ 30 the two are nearly identical. At DOF 29 the peak of t is 0.396 against 0.399 for Z. The slide's drawing exaggerates the gap for effect.

24slide

t-tests: simple example (one sample)

24t-tests – Simple Example

Test whether a sample of size n = 25 with mean x̄ = 79 and SD s = 10 was drawn at random from a population with mean μ = 75 and unknown SD.

t-statistic · sl. 24t = x − μs / √n = 79 − 7510 / √25 = 42 = 2

Result

sl. 24
Test
2-sided, SL α = 0.05, t distribution on 24 DOF (n − 1).
Critical values
−2.064 and 2.064
Decision
The calculated t = 2 does not exceed these values, so H₀ cannot be rejected with 95% confidence.
Note
"The confidence level is 1 − α."

outside slidesRe-computed: two-sided p = 0.057, just above 0.05, which agrees with the slide's decision. With σ known and a z-test, ±1.96 would have been the cut-off and 2 would have been significant. This is the heavier-tails point from sl. 22 in practice.

25–28slides

Paired sample t-test and the HCL training case

25Paired Sample t-test26Case Study: Paired Sample t-test27Paired Sample t-test in EXCEL28Paired and Independent Samples

With a paired sample t-test you make two measurements for each item (observation) in your sample, and each such set is a sample. CAUTION: these two samples are not independent of each other because of the pairing (sl. 25).

Case · sl. 26

HCL gives OTJ (on-the-job) training to a sample of employees. A training company claims the training "is sure to improve the work performance of HCL employees". HCL records performance for the sample before the training and for the same employees after the training. Is there a significant improvement? If so, the program is effective "and may be tried again in the future".

Ghosh's verdict · sl. 27

"tact = −15.656 < tcrit = 2.045. Also, p = 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁵ ≪ α = 0.05. We reject NH. Say with 95% confidence that the training has made a +ve impact on employee performance."

Trap · sl. 27

The comparison is written the wrong way round. −15.656 < 2.045 would on its own mean "do not reject". The rule compares the absolute value: |tact| = 15.656 > 2.045, so reject. The sign is negative only because Excel's Variable 1 is Before, so Before − After is negative. The p-value line gives the same verdict, and it never depends on the sign.

Paired vs independent samples

sl. 28
Paired
(Or dependent.) Same subjects, e.g. pre- and post-test measurements on the same people. They form matched data points: each measurement in one sample has a corresponding, unique measurement in the other.
Independent
(Or unpaired.) Different, unrelated groups, e.g. comparing men and women. There is no connection: observations in one group are unrelated to observations in the other.

outside slidesWhy pairing matters here: the Pearson correlation of 0.98 means good employees stay good. Pairing subtracts each person's baseline, so only the training effect (mean difference 12.9) is left against a small spread of differences (SD ≈ 4.5). Analyse the same 60 numbers as if they were two independent groups and the person-to-person spread (SD ≈ 23) swamps the effect: t ≈ −2.13, p ≈ 0.037. Try the "HCL paired as independent" preset in the lab.

29–31slides

The 2-sample t-test, boxplots and the HCL control group

292-Sample t-test30Boxplot in R and Python31Case Study: 2-Sample t-test

With a 2-sample t-test you want to determine whether there is a difference in means between two groups within the population. Two cases arise: 1. group variances are equal; 2. group variances are unequal. To see which, "you can perform a boxplot of the data to see if the variances are reasonably close to each other". "If you're unsure, go with the 2nd strategy" (unequal variances) (sl. 29).

R · RStudiosl. 30
boxplot(mtcars$mpg)
Pythonsl. 30
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
data = [12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 26, 28, 30, 35, 40, 65]
plt.boxplot(data)
plt.title(“My Boxplot")   # [sic: opening “ must be "]
plt.show()

outside slidesThe Python title line opens with a curly quote (“) and closes with a straight one ("). Typed as shown it is a SyntaxError; use plt.title("My Boxplot"). In that data, 65 lies beyond the upper whisker (Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 32.5 + 1.5 × 13 = 52 with matplotlib's default quartiles), so it plots as an outlier dot. To compare two groups' spreads, put both in one call: boxplot(mscore, fscore) in R, plt.boxplot([m, f]) in Python.

Case · sl. 31

HCL investigates the effect of an OTJ training program (footnote: "OTJ = On-the-job"). It samples 30 employees who have been through the training, the experimental group, and 30 who have not, the control group. All are examined and given a performance score.

32–34slides

Equal variance: the pooled t-test, and DoF

322-Sample t-test – Equal Variance – 1332-Sample t-test – Equal Variance – 234What's DoF?

Suppose the population variances are known, "somehow". Then you can use the normal distribution. REMEMBER: population variances are hardly ever known in practice. So you pool the sample variances and use the t distribution (sl. 32).

Pooled two-sample t · sl. 33t = (x − y) − (μx − μy)s √1/nx + 1/ny  follows  t(nx + ny − 2)
Pooled variance · sl. 33s² = (nx − 1)sx² + (ny − 1)sy²nx + ny − 2

Here x̄ and ȳ are the means of the two groups (your two samples) of sizes nx and ny. nx + ny − 2 is the degrees of freedom (DoF) of the t distribution, and s² is the pooled variance (sl. 33).

What's DoF?

sl. 34
Definition
Degrees of freedom (DoF) is the number of independent values in a sample that are free to vary when you compute a statistic: the number of pieces of information that can change without altering a calculated parameter or restriction.
Example
For a sample of size n, often DoF = n − 1. Why? "Because once a specific quantity, such as the sample mean, is known, the last value is no longer free to vary."
Pooled case
outside slidesEach group's mean uses up one value, so two groups give nx + ny − 2.
35–37slides

Worked example: new vs traditional pedagogy

35Example: Problem Setup36Example: Calculation37Example: Result
Group (sl. 35)MeanSDn
A: new pedagogyx̄₁ = 85s₁ = 5n₁ = 30
B: traditional pedagogyx̄₂ = 80s₂ = 4n₂ = 30 [slide: "(2)" → n₂]

H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ (no difference in mean test scores). H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (a difference exists). The question asks whether A gives higher scores, but the hypotheses are two-sided.

Step 1: pooled variance · sl. 36s² = (30 − 1)·25 + (30 − 1)·1630 + 30 − 2 = 725 + 46458 = 20.5
Step 2: t-stat · sl. 36t = 85 − 80√20.5 · (1/30 + 1/30) ≈ 4.28

Result

sl. 37
DoF
n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 58
Critical t
For a typical α = 0.05, roughly ±2.00 (exact: 2.0017).
Decision
4.28 > 2.00, so the result is statistically significant. Reject the null and conclude that the new pedagogy yields significantly different (here, higher) test scores.

outside slidesRe-computed: 1189 / 58 = 20.500; SE = √(20.5 × 0.0667) = 1.169; t = 4.277; p ≈ 0.00007. The 95% CI for μ₁ − μ₂ is 5 ± 2.0017 × 1.169 = (2.66, 7.34).

Ghosh's verdict · sl. 38

"tact = −1.214 < tcrit = 2.001. Also, p = 0.229 > α = 0.05. We fail to reject NH. Say with 95% confidence that difference between the two groups is purely by chance."

Trap · sl. 38

The decision is right (|−1.214| < 2.001 and p > 0.05), but the last sentence says more than the test can. Failing to reject H₀ means the data give no evidence of a difference. It does not prove, "with 95% confidence", that the difference is pure chance. B07 makes the same point: you never accept the null. outside slidesAlso, the sheet has a "Difference" column even though control and trained are different employees. Subtracting unrelated people's scores is meaningless here; it is left over from the paired sheet.

Unequal variance

sl. 39
Idea
The unequal variance case is similar to the equal variance case.
Before you run it
You should have "a fairly good idea or hunch" about the two groups' variances. If you have evidence to suspect that their variances are unequal, run the unequal variance test.
Excel
Just select the unequal variance test in Data Analysis. The dialog lists Histogram, Moving Average, Random Number Generation, Rank and Percentile, Regression, Sampling, t-Test: Paired Two Sample for Means, t-Test: Two-Sample Assuming Equal Variances, t-Test: Two-Sample Assuming Unequal Variances (highlighted), z-Test: Two Sample for Means.
In R
This is the Welch-Satterthwaite test, var.equal = F (TTest-2 sl. 12–14).
Ghosh · sl. 40

"The two-sample t-test is used to determine if two population means are equal. A common application is to test if a new process or treatment is superior to a current process or treatment."

Deck 2 of 2 · Lect-TTest-2 · 24 slides

t-test in R

Builds on TTest-1 (pooled vs unequal variance), B05/B06 (vectors with c(), var(), histograms) and B07 (p-value rule). Data are typed in as two vectors, not read from Data Files/. Every output below was re-run in R 4 and matches the slides to the last digit, except where the trap box says otherwise.

1–5slides

Set-up: the car package and the score vectors

1The t-test2t-test in R3The "car" Package42-sample t-tests – 15Create Vectors mscore and fscore

First install the "car" package, then load it into the current R session (sl. 3). It supplies leveneTest(), used in sl. 16–21. The task is to conduct an independent samples t-test in R with homogeneity of variance (variances the same for the two groups, "the equal variance test"), on male and female scores (sl. 4).

Rsl. 3, 5
> install.packages("car")
> library("car")

> mscore <- c(25,26,19,27,24,24,28,29,21,28,
              22,25,26,25,20,23,29,25,22,22)
> fscore <- c(30,27,24,26,28,32,24,25,29,25,
              31,30,21,28,22,22,27,27,26,30)
Python equivalentoutside slides
# no install step: scipy ships the tests
from scipy import stats
m = [25,26,19,27,24,24,28,29,21,28,
     22,25,26,25,20,23,29,25,22,22]
f = [30,27,24,26,28,32,24,25,29,25,
     31,30,21,28,22,22,27,27,26,30]

NOTE: the c() function creates a vector in R; the 1st is assigned to mscore and the 2nd to fscore. Each has 20 values. The slide asks: what is H₀ here, and what is H₁? outside slidesH₀: μmale = μfemale (difference in means = 0, the mu = 0 argument); H₁: μmale ≠ μfemale (two-sided).

6–8slides

Equal-variance t.test() and its output

62-sample t-tests – 272-sample t-tests – 3 (Output)82-sample t-tests – 4
R · 2-sided H₁, 95% CIsl. 6
t.test(mscore, fscore,
       alternative = c("two.sided"),
       mu = 0, paired = F,
       var.equal = T, conf.level = 0.95)
Python equivalentoutside slides
stats.ttest_ind(m, f, equal_var=True)
# t = -2.3016, p = 0.02693, df = 38
ArgumentMeaning
alternative = c("two.sided")H₁ is ≠. outside slidesThe other options are "less" and "greater" for one-tailed tests.
mu = 0Hypothesised difference in means under H₀.
paired = FIndependent samples. outside slidespaired = T runs the pre-post test of TTest-1 sl. 25–27.
var.equal = TPool the variances (TTest-1 sl. 33), df = n₁ + n₂ − 2.
conf.level = 0.95Confidence level of the reported interval, 1 − α.
Two Sample t-test data: mscore and fscore t = -2.3016, df = 38, p-value = 0.02693 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: -4.1350542 -0.2649458 sample estimates: mean of x mean of y 24.5 26.7

Reading the output

sl. 6–7: "Correctly interpret it"
t, df
t = −2.3016 on 38 df (20 + 20 − 2). Negative because the first vector (male) has the smaller mean.
p-value
0.02693 < 0.05: reject H₀. Mean scores of men and women differ significantly at the 5% level.
95% CI
(−4.135, −0.265) for μmale − μfemale. It excludes 0, which is the same verdict as p < 0.05. outside slidesWomen score between about 0.26 and 4.1 points higher.
Estimates
Mean of x (male) 24.5; mean of y (female) 26.7; difference −2.2.

Sl. 8 then computes each group's variance, var(mscore) and var(fscore), and asks "What's your conclusion from this?" The slide shows no output. outside slidesThe values are 8.474 and 9.800 (SDs 2.91 and 3.13). They are close, so the equal-variance test was reasonable. Sl. 15–24 test this formally.

9–11slides

Shapiro-Wilk normality test and histograms

9Shapiro-Wilks [→ Shapiro-Wilk] Normality Test102-sample t-tests – 5112-sample t-tests – 6

Next, test data normality. The Shapiro-Wilk normality test "tries to detect departures from normality". It rejects the hypothesis of normality when p ≤ 0.05. Do the samples pass? Also inspect graphically (sl. 9).

Rsl. 10–11
> shapiro.test(mscore)
W = 0.96497, p-value = 0.6472
> shapiro.test(fscore)
W = 0.96914, p-value = 0.7367
> hist(mscore)
> hist(fscore)
Python equivalentoutside slides
stats.shapiro(m)   # W 0.96497, p 0.6472
stats.shapiro(f)   # W 0.96914, p 0.7367
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.hist(m); plt.show()

Reading it: both p-values are well above 0.05, so normality is not rejected and both samples pass. That supports the t-test's normality assumption. Sl. 11 histograms: "Histogram of mscore" (x-axis 18–30) and "Histogram of fscore" (x-axis 20–32), both roughly single-peaked with no long tail. "Do these appear to be normal?" Roughly, yes, for 20 points each.

outside slidesNote the direction. Here H₀ is "the data are normal", so a large p is the good outcome. In the t-test, a small p is the "interesting" result. Exams like to flip these.

12–14slides

Welch-Satterthwaite t-test (unequal variances)

12Welch-Satterthwaite t-test132-sample t-tests – 7142-sample t-tests – 8 (Output)

The Welch-Satterthwaite t-test treats t′ as following a t distribution, but not with dof = n₁ + n₂ − 2. If variances are unequal, a different dof must be employed ("a bit complicated, right?"):

Welch–Satterthwaite dof · sl. 12dof = ( S₁²/n₁ + S₂²/n₂ )²( S₁²/n₁ )² / (n₁ − 1) + ( S₂²/n₂ )² / (n₂ − 1)
Rsl. 13
> t.test(mscore, fscore,
         alternative = c("two.sided"), mu = 0,
         paired = F, var.equal = F,
         conf.level = 0.95)
Python equivalentoutside slides
stats.ttest_ind(m, f, equal_var=False)
# t = -2.3016, p = 0.02697, df = 37.80
Welch Two Sample t-test data: mscore and fscore t = -2.3016, df = 37.801, p-value = 0.02697 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: -4.135389 -0.264611 sample estimates: mean of x mean of y 24.5 26.7

Reading it: the conclusion is unchanged: p = 0.02697 < 0.05, reject H₀. Only the df changes, a fractional 37.801 instead of 38, and with it the p-value and CI in the fourth decimal. outside slidest is identical because with equal group sizes (20 and 20) the pooled and Welch standard errors are the same number. With unequal sizes and unequal variances they diverge. Welch is R's default when var.equal is omitted, which matches TTest-1 sl. 29: "If you're unsure, go with the 2nd strategy".

15–19, 23slides

Testing homogeneity of variances

15Testing Homogeneity of Variances162-sample t-tests – 917Levene Test for Homogeneity of Variance18Fligner-Killeen Test for Homogeneity of Variance19F Test for Homogeneity of Variance23The Var Test

There are three popular tests for the homogeneity of variances. "Homogeneity" means "equality". They are the Levene test, the Fligner-Killeen test and the Var test (sl. 15). The hypotheses are H₀: σ₁² = σ₂²; H₁: σ₁² ≠ σ₂² (sl. 16).

R · as on the slidesl. 16
> leveneTest(mscore, fscore, center = mean)
> leveneTest(mscore, fscore, center = median)
> fligner.test(mscore, fscore)
> var.test(mscore, fscore)

Levene sl. 17

Determines whether the variances of different groups are similar or significantly different. Null: all group variances are equal. Alternative: at least two group variances are different. It computes a statistic based on the absolute deviations from the group means, then a p-value. p ≥ 0.05: null not rejected, no significant difference in variances. p < 0.05: null rejected, the variances differ.

Fligner-Killeen sl. 18

A nonparametric test of homogeneity of variances across groups. Useful with non-normal data distributions, when traditional tests fail to meet the assumptions needed for valid results. In such cases use it "as a reliable alternative, allowing for a more accurate assessment of variance homogeneity across groups".

F test / Var test sl. 19, 23

Determines whether the variances of two populations are equal. It computes the ratio of the larger sample variance to the smaller (the F-statistic) and compares it with critical values from an F-distribution. It assumes the data are normally and independently distributed. The larger variance goes in the numerator to ensure a right-tailed test. var.test performs this F-test on two samples from normal populations, evaluating whether two independent groups' variances are statistically equal.

outside slidesWhich to use: the F / var test is the most powerful when data are normal, but it is fragile otherwise. Levene with center = median (also called Brown-Forsythe) and Fligner-Killeen are robust to non-normal data. Here Shapiro-Wilk passed (sl. 10), so all three are fair.

20–22, 24slides

The homogeneity outputs, and what they should say

202-sample t-tests – 10212-sample t-tests – 11222-sample t-tests – 12242-sample t-tests – 13
SlideCallOutput on slidepSlide verdict
20leveneTest(…, center = mean)Df group 10, resid 9; F = 14.242 ***0.0002369Reject equal variances
21leveneTest(…, center = median)Df 10 / 9; F = 2.7872 .0.06922Do not reject
22fligner.test(mscore, fscore)Fligner-Killeen:med χ² = 13.493, df = 100.1974Do not reject
24var.test(mscore, fscore)F = 0.86466, num df 19, denom df 19; 95% CI 0.3422436 – 2.1845252; ratio of variances 0.86466170.7545Do not reject

Signif. codes printed under the Levene tables: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1. The slides pose the outputs without stating a conclusion. Read by the sl. 17 rule, Levene-mean (p = 0.0002) says the variances differ, while Levene-median, Fligner and the var test say they do not. var.test's ratio 0.865 = 8.474 / 9.800, and its CI contains 1, so the variances are equal and var.equal = T (sl. 6) was justified.

Trap · sl. 16, 20–22 (checked by re-running in R and scipy)

The Levene and Fligner calls are used wrongly, which is why they disagree with var.test. Both functions take (values, group), so leveneTest(mscore, fscore) treats the female scores as a grouping factor. fscore has 11 distinct values, giving 11 "groups", hence Df 10 and 20 − 11 = 9 residual df. The test is then asking whether male scores vary equally across "female score levels", which means nothing. A real two-group test has df 1 and 38.

Stack the data with a group label instead:

R · correct calloutside slides
score  <- c(mscore, fscore)
gender <- factor(rep(c("M","F"), each = 20))
leveneTest(score, gender, center = mean)    # F = 0.113, p = 0.738
leveneTest(score, gender, center = median)  # F = 0.123, p = 0.727
fligner.test(score, gender)                 # chi2 = 0.107, df 1, p = 0.744
# Python: stats.levene(m, f, center='mean'), stats.fligner(m, f)

Run correctly, all four tests agree: p ≈ 0.73–0.75, equal variances. var.test(mscore, fscore) is the one call on the slide that is correct as written, because it takes two samples. In an exam, quote the slide's numbers if asked what the slide shows, but know that the honest conclusion is "variances equal".

outside slidesSl. 19 says the larger variance goes in the numerator, but R's var.test always puts the first argument on top, here 8.474 / 9.800 = 0.865 < 1, and runs a two-sided test. The slide describes the hand method with a table of F critical values; R does not need it.

Which t-test?

Both decks on one page
1 · What is being compared?
One sample vs a known μ

One-sample t

t = (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n), df = n − 1. Population SD unknown. (TTest-1 sl. 24)

outside slidesR t.test(x, mu = 75); Python stats.ttest_1samp(x, 75).

Same items measured twice

Paired t

Pre-post / dependent / matched / repeated measure. Samples are not independent. df = n − 1 pairs. Excel: "t-Test: Paired Two Sample for Means". (TTest-1 sl. 7, 18, 25–28)

outside slidesR paired = T; Python stats.ttest_rel.

Two unrelated groups

Two-sample t

Independent / control vs experimental. Go to step 2. (TTest-1 sl. 8–13, 29)

2 · Two independent groups: check the assumptions
Normal?

Shapiro-Wilk + histogram

shapiro.test(): p ≤ 0.05 rejects normality. Also hist(). (TTest-2 sl. 9–11)

Equal variances?

Boxplot, then a test

Boxplot to eyeball spreads (TTest-1 sl. 29–30). Then Levene (car::leveneTest), Fligner-Killeen (non-normal data) or var.test (F, normal data). p ≥ 0.05: treat as equal. (TTest-2 sl. 15–24)

3 · Pick the version
Variances equal

Pooled t

s² = [(n₁−1)s₁² + (n₂−1)s₂²]/(n₁+n₂−2); df = n₁ + n₂ − 2. R var.equal = T; Excel "Assuming Equal Variances". (TTest-1 sl. 32–38; TTest-2 sl. 6–7)

Unequal, or unsure

Welch t

Welch-Satterthwaite dof (fractional). R var.equal = F; Excel "Assuming Unequal Variances". "If you're unsure, go with the 2nd strategy." (TTest-1 sl. 29, 39; TTest-2 sl. 12–14)

Population variances known

Normal (z)

"Hardly ever known in practice." Excel "z-Test: Two Sample for Means". Large samples (n > 30) also make t ≈ normal. (TTest-1 sl. 20, 32, 39)

Quick revision

The two decks on one screen

The argument in ten lines

  1. The t-test is a top-down DSA method built on hypothesis testing (T1 sl. 14).
  2. Problem 1, pre-post: same group measured before and after an intervention → paired / dependent t-test (T1 sl. 3–7).
  3. Problem 2, two groups: control vs experimental, line A vs line B → independent / two-sample t-test (T1 sl. 8–13).
  4. HT: H₀ = no effect; H₁ = interesting effect; α = P(reject a true H₀); p = P(data this extreme | H₀) (T1 sl. 15–17).
  5. Gosset ("Student"), Guinness, Dublin, 1908: small samples, unknown σ → the t distribution (T1 sl. 19–21).
  6. t is symmetric about 0 with heavier tails, shaped by DOF = n − 1, ≈ normal by n > 30 (T1 sl. 20–23).
  7. Paired samples are not independent; HCL training: t = −15.66, p ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ → training works (T1 sl. 25–27).
  8. Two samples: equal variances → pooled s² and df n₁ + n₂ − 2; unequal or unsure → unequal-variance (Welch) test (T1 sl. 29–39).
  9. In R: t.test(…, var.equal = T/F); male vs female scores differ, p ≈ 0.027 either way (T2 sl. 6–14).
  10. Check assumptions: Shapiro-Wilk for normality; Levene / Fligner-Killeen / var.test for equal variances (T2 sl. 9–24).

Key quotes

"It's appropriate when your sample size is small and you do not know the true population SD."T1 sl. 21

"CAUTION: These two samples are not independent of each other because of the pairing."T1 sl. 25

"If you're unsure, go with the 2nd strategy."T1 sl. 29

"The problem is that population variances are hardly ever known in practice."T1 sl. 32

"The test rejects the hypothesis of normality when p ≤ 0.05."T2 sl. 9

Terms

Pre-post application
Same group measured before (pre-test) and after (post-test) an intervention.
Paired / dependent / matched / repeated-measure t
t-test on two related measurements per item.
Independent / two-sample t
t-test comparing means of two separate, unrelated groups.
Control / experimental group
Without / with the intervention; comparison isolates cause and effect.
Placebo
Inactive substance given as if it were a real treatment.
Significance level α
Probability of incorrectly rejecting a true null.
p-value
Probability of data as extreme as observed if H₀ were true.
t distribution
Student's t: bell-shaped, heavier tails, depends on DOF.
Degrees of freedom
Number of independent values free to vary when computing a statistic.
Pooled variance
Weighted average of the two sample variances, used when variances are equal.
Welch-Satterthwaite
Unequal-variance t-test with its own (fractional) dof.
Homogeneity of variance
Equality of group variances.
Shapiro-Wilk
Normality test; p ≤ 0.05 rejects normality.
Levene
Equal-variance test on absolute deviations from group means (or medians).
Fligner-Killeen
Nonparametric equal-variance test, for non-normal data.
F / var test
Ratio of two sample variances against an F-distribution; needs normal data.

Names and things

  • William Sealy Gosset ("Student"), Englishman, Guinness brewery, Dublin, 1908 (T1 sl. 19).
  • HCL: OTJ training, paired case (sl. 26–27) and control-vs-trained case (sl. 31, 38).
  • SNU: teaching-method studies, pre-post (sl. 6) and Method A vs B for 2nd-year BMS (sl. 12).
  • car package: leveneTest() (T2 sl. 3).
  • Excel Data Analysis ToolPak: three t-test entries and a z-test (T1 sl. 39).

Traps

  • Compare |t| with tcrit; sl. 27 writes "−15.656 < 2.045" and still (correctly) rejects.
  • Failing to reject ≠ proving the difference is chance (sl. 38's wording).
  • Shapiro-Wilk: large p is good (normal). t-test: small p is the finding.
  • leveneTest(mscore, fscore) and fligner.test(mscore, fscore) misuse fscore as a group: df 10 is the giveaway. Correctly run, p ≈ 0.74.
  • Same-size groups give the same t for pooled and Welch; only df and p shift (T2 sl. 7 vs 14).
  • The SNU teaching example is paired in sl. 6 but independent in sl. 12: decide by who is measured.
  • Python boxplot line on sl. 30 has a curly opening quote: SyntaxError as typed.

Self-test

Answer aloud, then reveal
—

The t-test (TTest-1)

1Describe the "1st type of problem" the t-test solves, and give the deck's three examples.

A system is in some state, something external happens, and its condition improves or worsens: is the change significant? Examples: training → job performance; drug → memory scores; new teaching method → test scores. (sl. 3–6)

2Give three other names for the pre-post t-test, and say what it compares.

Paired sample t-test, dependent t-test (sl. 7); also matched sample or repeated measure t-test (sl. 18). It compares the average values of two related measurements, usually before and after an intervention on the same group.

3What do the control and experimental groups do, and what does comparing them establish?

The experimental group receives the intervention; the control does not. Comparing them isolates the intervention's impact and establishes a cause-and-effect relationship. (sl. 9)

4Define a placebo, and say which test the cancer-drug trial needs.

An inactive substance, like a sugar pill, given as if it were a real treatment. Two separate groups (drug vs placebo) → independent / two-sample t-test. (sl. 10, 13)

5Define the significance level and the p-value as the deck does.

SL (α): the probability of incorrectly rejecting a true null (e.g. 0.05). p-value: the probability of observing something as extreme as the sample data if the null were true. (sl. 17)

6Who developed the t-test, when, where, and why?

William Sealy Gosset, publishing as "Student", in 1908, while at the Guinness brewery in Dublin. Large-sample techniques were not useful for the small samples he met. (sl. 19)

7When is the t distribution appropriate, and when is the normal used instead?

When the sample is small and the true population SD is unknown (sl. 21). For a sample mean with n > 30 the normal is usually applied (sl. 20, 22).

8List the four characteristics of the t distribution.

Bell-shaped and symmetric about 0; heavier tails (shorter, flatter middle, so extreme values more likely); shape set by DOF = n − 1; approaches the standard normal as n and DOF grow, usually by n > 30. (sl. 22)

9n = 25, x̄ = 79, s = 10, μ = 75. Compute t and decide at α = 0.05 (two-sided).

t = (79 − 75)/(10/√25) = 4/2 = 2. Critical values on 24 DOF are ±2.064; 2 does not exceed them, so H₀ cannot be rejected. (sl. 24)

10In the HCL paired Excel output, what are t, df, the two-tail p and t-critical, and what is the conclusion?

t = −15.6555, df = 29, p = 1.11E−15, t crit two-tail = 2.04523. |t| far exceeds 2.045 and p ≪ 0.05: reject H₀; the training had a positive impact. (sl. 27)

11How do you decide between the equal- and unequal-variance two-sample tests, and what if you're unsure?

Draw a boxplot to see if the variances are reasonably close (sl. 29), or use a hunch or evidence about the variances (sl. 39). If unsure, use the unequal-variance test. (sl. 29)

12Write the pooled variance and the DoF of the pooled t-test.

s² = [(nₓ − 1)sₓ² + (n_y − 1)s_y²]/(nₓ + n_y − 2); DoF = nₓ + n_y − 2. (sl. 33)

13Define degrees of freedom and explain why a sample often has n − 1.

The number of independent values free to vary when computing a statistic. Once the sample mean is known, the last value is no longer free to vary. (sl. 34)

14Pedagogy example: A (85, 5, 30) vs B (80, 4, 30). Find s², t, df and the decision.

s² = (29·25 + 29·16)/58 = 1189/58 = 20.5. t = 5/√(20.5·(1/30 + 1/30)) ≈ 4.28. df = 58, critical ≈ ±2.00. 4.28 > 2.00 → reject H₀: the new pedagogy gives higher scores. (sl. 35–37)

t-test in R (TTest-2)

15Which package must be installed and loaded, and for which function?

install.packages("car") then library("car"); it provides leveneTest(). (sl. 3, 16)

16State H₀ and H₁ for the mscore vs fscore test.

H₀: the true difference in mean scores (male − female) is 0. H₁: it is not 0 (two-sided). (sl. 5–7)

17Write the R call for a two-sided, equal-variance, 95% independent t-test.

t.test(mscore, fscore, alternative = c("two.sided"), mu = 0, paired = F, var.equal = T, conf.level = 0.95) (sl. 6)

18Interpret: t = −2.3016, df = 38, p = 0.02693, 95% CI (−4.135, −0.265), means 24.5 and 26.7.

p < 0.05 and the CI excludes 0 → reject H₀. Male and female mean scores differ significantly; the female mean is higher by 2.2. (sl. 7)

19What does the Shapiro-Wilk test do, when does it reject, and what did it find here?

It detects departures from normality and rejects normality when p ≤ 0.05. Here p = 0.6472 (male) and 0.7367 (female): both samples pass as normal. (sl. 9–10)

20How does the Welch-Satterthwaite test differ from the pooled test? Write its dof.

It does not use dof = n₁ + n₂ − 2. dof = (S₁²/n₁ + S₂²/n₂)² / [(S₁²/n₁)²/(n₁ − 1) + (S₂²/n₂)²/(n₂ − 1)]. In R, var.equal = F. (sl. 12–13)

21The Welch output gives df = 37.801, p = 0.02697. What changed from the pooled run, and does the conclusion change?

Only the df (38 → 37.801) and the p and CI in the 4th decimal; t is still −2.3016. The conclusion is the same: reject H₀. (sl. 7, 14)

22Name the three homogeneity-of-variance tests and say what "homogeneity" means.

Levene, Fligner-Killeen and the Var (F) test. Homogeneity means equality. (sl. 15)

23State Levene's null, alternative and decision rule.

Null: all group variances are equal. Alternative: at least two differ. p ≥ 0.05 → not rejected (no significant difference); p < 0.05 → rejected. It uses absolute deviations from the group means. (sl. 17)

24When should you prefer Fligner-Killeen to the F test?

When the data are not normal. Fligner-Killeen is nonparametric; the F test assumes normally and independently distributed data. (sl. 18–19)

25How is the F statistic built, according to sl. 19?

The ratio of the larger sample variance to the smaller, compared with critical values of an F-distribution; the larger goes on top to make the test right-tailed. (R's var.test instead puts the first argument on top and tests two-sided.)

26Read the var.test output: F = 0.86466, df 19/19, p = 0.7545, CI 0.342–2.185.

p > 0.05 and the CI for the variance ratio contains 1 → do not reject equal variances. The pooled (var.equal = T) test was appropriate. (sl. 24)

27The sl. 20 Levene output shows "Df 10" and p = 0.0002. Why is that suspicious?

Two groups should give 1 numerator df. leveneTest(mscore, fscore) treats fscore's 11 distinct values as groups. Run correctly on stacked data with a gender factor, p = 0.738: equal variances, matching var.test. (Re-run outside the slides.)

28Put the whole R workflow in order for two independent samples.

Create the vectors (c()) → state H₀/H₁ → check normality (shapiro.test, hist) → check variances (var, leveneTest, fligner.test, var.test) → run t.test with var.equal = T (equal) or F (unequal) → read p, CI and means. The slides run t.test first and checks after (sl. 6–24); the logic is checks first.

Method

  • Re-extracted both PDFs page by page with === p. N === slide markers (the cached extracts had none).
  • Rendered all 64 slides as contact sheets. Read the formula slides (sl. 22, 24, 33, 35–37; T2 sl. 12, 16) from the images, because the text layer drops every t, μ, σ, x̄ and fraction. Read the Excel sheets (sl. 27, 38) at 220 dpi.
  • Re-ran every TTest-2 command in R and the scipy equivalents in Python. All outputs match the slides. The Levene/Fligner calls were also re-run with a proper group factor.
  • Built a slide-by-slide inventory before drafting, then ran the coverage script on each deck and read each flagged line against the page.

Why the script flagged lines that are covered

  • Dropped symbols: lines such as "The -test", "− = ⁄" and "!" are the text layer's rendering of t, the formulas and H₀, transcribed here from the images.
  • Questions on slides ("What's your output?", "Correctly interpret it", "Do these appear to be normal?") are answered on the page rather than repeated word for word.
  • Paraphrased bullets carrying the same content in shorter words.

What the first draft missed (now fixed)

  • Six example and definition cards (sl. 3, 4, 6, 11, 12, 18) were paraphrased so loosely that they scored 0.67. They now follow the slide wording ("in many fields and disciplines", "an education study", "two important actions, among others").
  • Two outside-slides numbers were wrong in the draft and were caught by recomputing: the t peak at DOF 29 (0.396, not 0.394) and the boxplot upper fence on sl. 30 (52, not 51.75).

Left out on purpose

  • The Shiv Nadar University logo (sl. 1 of both decks).
  • Nine of the 30 rows of the sl. 27 sheet and ten of the 30 rows of the sl. 38 sheet. Most are not visible on the slides; of those visible, a sample is shown, and the summary statistics cover all 30.
  • Nothing examinable was dropped.

Limits of the check

  • The script matches words, not meaning. A slide idea in different words scores lower, and a word that appears elsewhere on the page can hide a gap. Flagged lines were read by hand.
  • Additions marked outside slides include: the Python equivalents, p-values and CIs the slides do not print, the var() values, the paired-as-independent comparison, the corrected Levene/Fligner calls, and the "Which t-test?" chart's R/Python names for paired and one-sample tests. The lecturer may phrase or weight these differently. Check against the slides before quoting them in a test.
  • The back-solved SD of differences in the HCL paired preset (≈ 4.513) comes from t = −15.6555 and n = 30, since the slide shows only 21 of 30 rows.
